p.x:
Last Saturday was my mum's fiftieth birthday, and we had a surprise party for her. My dad, my sister and I planned it for weeks. We bought lots of balloons and flowers, and my sister made a big card.
In the afternoon, we took Mum to the cinema. While we were out, our friends came to the house and put up the balloons. When we came home, everyone shouted, "Surprise!" Mum was so happy that she cried.
We all gave her gifts. I wrapped mine in gold paper. It was a silver ring with her name on it. My dad said, "Congratulations on fifty wonderful years!" Then everyone lifted their glasses and said, "Cheers!"

Last month, my cousin Nan got married. It was a beautiful day. In the morning, there was a traditional Thai ceremony with the families. In the evening, there was a big reception in a hotel.
The hotel was full of decorations: white flowers, lights and candles. Nan looked lovely in her white dress and veil, and she carried a bouquet of pink roses. Her two bridesmaids wore pink, too. The dress code for guests was formal, so I wore a suit.
The caterer served a huge banquet with fifteen dishes. After dinner, the best man made a toast to the newlyweds, and Nan and her husband read their vows. A photographer took pictures all evening, and later a DJ played music. Everyone was on the dance floor; even Nan's in-laws danced! As they left, we threw confetti over them.
I love special occasions. Last year, I went to my brother's graduation and my grandfather's retirement party, and next month, I'm going to a school reunion. But weddings are the best, because there's always a feast, and each guest can bring their spouse or partner.

In many cultures, weddings are among the most important events in a person's life, and they can also be among the most expensive. In Thailand, it is customary for the groom's family to give a dowry, known as sin sod, to the bride's parents, and the size of this payment can reflect the family's status. Couples often consult an astrologer to choose an auspicious date, and some superstitions advise against marrying in certain months.
In recent years, the scale of celebrations has grown dramatically. Social media has encouraged lavish weddings with designer dresses, luxury venues and hundreds of guests, and the festivities may last several days. Critics argue that such extravagant spending places enormous pressure on young couples, some of whom take on debt that lasts long after the honeymoon.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, a counter-trend has emerged. Some couples now choose a small ceremony at a register office followed by a simple meal with close family. A few even elope, marrying in secret to avoid the cost and the complicated etiquette that large weddings involve. Others donate the money they would have spent to charity.
Whatever the scale, researchers who study marriage note that there is little evidence that the cost of a wedding predicts the success of the matrimony that follows. In fact, one well-known study found that couples who spent the most were slightly more likely to divorce. What matters most, it seems, is not the size of the party but the commitment behind the vows.
